title: Project: The Shor Code Under Noise
summary: Build the nine-qubit Shor code, compute its logical failure probability under depolarizing noise exactly, and find the physical error rate below which encoding helps.
objectives: Build and check a Shor-code decoder against every single-qubit Pauli error
Count the error patterns that defeat the code and turn the count into an exact failure probability
Compare the encoded qubit with a bare one and find the error rate where the two are equal
mission: Whether nine qubits beat one is a question of counting, and you will answer it exactly. Part 1: complete encode() and decode() as in lesson 4.4, so that qubit 0 returns to |ψ⟩ after an X, Y or Z error on any one of the nine qubits. Part 2: define logical_pauli(error), which takes a list of nine letters from I, X, Y, Z (error[q] acts on qubit q, applied between encoding and decoding) and returns the Pauli that is left on the logical qubit after majority-vote decoding. Part 3: define logical_failure(p), the probability that the logical Pauli is not I when every qubit independently suffers the depolarizing channel with probability p (I with probability 1 − p; X, Y, Z with probability p/3 each), and bare_failure(p) for one unprotected qubit. Part 4: store in p_star the smallest p > 0 at which logical_failure(p) = bare_failure(p), to within 0.003.

prediction.question: At small p, halving the physical error rate from p = 0.01 to p = 0.005 changes the logical failure probability of the Shor code by what factor?
options: It falls about four times, since the smallest failing patterns have two errors
It falls about two times, like the bare qubit
It falls about eight times, since the code has distance 3
prediction.explanation: The code corrects every single-qubit error, but some pairs of errors fail: of the 324 patterns with errors on exactly two qubits, 144 do, namely two X or Y errors in one block (36 patterns) and one Y or Z error in each of two blocks (108 patterns). Each has probability (p/3)², so p_L ≈ 144p²/9 = 16p², and halving p divides it by four (the exact values at 0.01 and 0.005 are 1.54 × 10⁻³ and 3.9 × 10⁻⁴). Distance 3 means every pair of errors is detected, not that every pair is corrected, and the Shor code does not correct all pairs, so the leading term is p², not p³.

hints: Build the circuit as in lesson 4.4 first. For the counting parts, ask what a block of three qubits can do to its leader: when does the inner vote fail, and when does a phase flip reach the leader?

In one block, the vote fails when at least two qubits carry X or Y, and the leader picks up a Z when an odd number of qubits carry Y or Z. Across the blocks, an odd number of failed votes is a logical Z, and an odd phase in at least two blocks is a logical X. Both together make Y.

Each block has 4³ = 64 patterns, with probability (1 − p)^(number of I) × (p/3)^(number of X, Y, Z). Add them up by effect (vote fails or not, Z parity odd or even), combine three blocks, and sum every combination whose logical Pauli is not I. For p_star, logical_failure(p) − p is negative just above 0 and positive after the crossover, so a grid or bisection finds it.
